result:
The moon is leaving. Not dramatically—it drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther away each year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow. But over deep time, the separation adds up.

When the moon was young, it hung much closer, and Earth spun faster—a day may have lasted only four hours. The tidal bulges the moon raised acted as brakes, slowing our rotation while flinging the moon outward: a cosmic exchange, trading the length of our days for the moon's distance. We've been paying this tithe for four and a half billion years.

Here's the quiet consequence: total solar eclipses are on borrowed time. The moon is about 400 times smaller than the sun and also about 400 times closer—a coincidence so exact that it blots the sun out perfectly, revealing the corona like a black flower. But the moon recedes while the sun does not, and in roughly 600 million years it will appear too small to cover the sun's face. Totality will end.

No one will miss it, in the way no one misses anything that fades across such spans. But consider: you live in the brief window when the geometry works, when you can stand in the moon's shadow, feel the air cool, and hear the birds go suddenly quiet. The eclipse is not a permanent feature of existence. It is an event. And we happen to be awake for it, which seems like reason enough to stand in the next shadow that passes over the Earth.
